what_its_for: Voclosporin is used to treat lupus nephritis, which is a type of kidney disease caused by lupus (an autoimmune condition where your immune system attacks your own body). This medicine helps calm down your immune system to protect your kidneys from further damage.
how_to_take: Take voclosporin by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or open them. You can take this medicine with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time. Take it at the same times every day to keep a steady amount in your body. This medicine is usually taken twice a day, about 12 hours apart.
dosing: The usual dose is 23.7 mg (which is 3 capsules) taken twice a day — once in the morning and once in the evening, about 12 hours apart. Your doctor may adjust your dose if you have kidney problems or if you are taking certain other medicines. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if there are more than 4 hours before your next scheduled dose. If your next dose is less than 4 hours away, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store voclosporin capsules at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Protect the capsules from moisture and heat. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it past the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid eating grapefruit or drinking grapefruit juice while taking this medicine, as it can cause your body to absorb too much of the drug and increase side effects. Avoid pomelos and Seville oranges for the same reason. Do not receive live vaccines (such as live flu vaccine, MMR, or chickenpox vaccine) while on this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, since this medicine lowers your immune system. Limit sun exposure and use sunscreen, as this medicine may increase your risk of skin cancer.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: signs of infection such as fever, chills, sore throat, or unusual tiredness; decreased urination or swelling in your legs or ankles that may signal kidney problems; numbness, tingling, or tremors (shaking); high blood pressure or severe headache; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of high potassium such as muscle weakness or irregular heartbeat; stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting that does not go away; or any unusual changes in your vision.
when_it_works: Voclosporin starts working in your body right away, but it may take several weeks to months before you notice improvements in your kidney function and lupus nephritis symptoms. Most studies showed meaningful benefits within 3 to 6 months of starting treatment. It is very important to keep taking this medicine even if you feel well, as stopping suddenly can worsen your condition.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment. If your kidneys are severely affected, your dose may need to be reduced or the medicine may not be recommended. Liver problems: This medicine should be used with caution if you have liver disease, as your dose may need adjustment. Pregnancy: Do not use voclosporin during pregnancy, as it may harm your unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for a period after stopping. Talk to your doctor before becoming pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine, as it may pass into breast milk and harm your baby. Older adults: Use with caution, as older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as kidney problems and infections. Children: The safety and effectiveness of voclosporin in children under 18 years old have not been established.
